input_signals.name: Profit Trend Minus Debt Build
input_signals.expression: SUB(RANK(TREND(RATIO(oiadp, at), 5)), RANK(GROWTH(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Improving operating profitability that is achieved without expanding the balance-sheet debt stock reflects genuine operating improvement; improving reported profit accompanied by rapid debt accumulation reflects leveraged, low-quality expansion that mean-reverts.
input_signals.reasoning: A five-year trend in operating income to assets captures the direction of operating strength as a state variable, while one-year growth in total interest-bearing debt captures the financing route used to get there. The rank difference rewards internally financed profit improvement and penalizes debt-financed profit improvement, an interaction that neither the trend nor leverage growth captures alone.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( rank( trend( ratio( oiadp, at ), 5 ) ), rank( growth( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Payout Signal Amplified By Cash Profitability
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(oancf, at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvt), sstk), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Net shareholder payout is informative only in proportion to the cash-generating capacity behind it: among cash-rich firms, distributions credibly reveal durable underpriced cash flow, while the same distribution from a cash-poor firm is uninformative (or liquidation), and the same *negative* payout (net issuance) from a cash-rich firm is a strong negative signal.
input_signals.reasoning: The financing leg is industry-demeaned and winsorized so it is centered at zero, which means the profitability rank acts purely as an amplitude gate rather than as an additive anomaly leg — a firm at any profitability level with median payout scores zero, so the composite cannot inherit the standalone cash-profitability premium. Because the sign of the signal is set entirely by the payout leg and its magnitude by profitability, the construct is non-monotone in profitability (high ROA pushes the signal up for repurchasers and down for issuers), which is the genuine interaction the critic asked for.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( oancf, at ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( prstkc, dvt ), sstk ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Unnecessary Issuance By Cash-Generative Firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3), 0.05), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: External capital raising is most diagnostic of overvaluation or concealed funding needs when the firm has demonstrated three years of solid internal cash generation and therefore has no visible need for outside money; among such firms, heavy gross issuance predicts low returns, whereas issuance by cash-poor firms is a mundane necessity with little information content.
input_signals.reasoning: The hard gate INDICATOR(MA(oancf/at,3), 0.05) is binary, so the signal cannot be increasing in profitability — it is exactly zero for all firms below the persistent-cash-generation threshold and equal to the (mean-zero) industry-standardized issuance intensity above it, eliminating the sign contradiction the critic identified. Using gross issuance (sstk + dltis) rather than net flows isolates the act of tapping capital markets, and the three-year smoothing of cash profitability ensures the conditioning state reflects an established funding position rather than one good year.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ), 0.05 ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( add( sstk, dltis ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Internal Funding Share Of Total Capital
input_signals.expression: MA(RATIO(oancf, ADD(ABS(oancf), ADD(sstk, dltis))), 3)
input_signals.hypothesis: The fraction of a firm's total funding that comes from its own operations, rather than from newly issued equity and debt, measures self-sufficiency; self-funded firms are underpriced cash generators, while firms whose funding mix is dominated by external issuance are either overvalued or capital-dependent.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the flawed shrinkage form with a single bounded ratio in [-1, 1] whose numerator is the profitability theme and whose denominator adds the financing theme, so profitability and financing enter one economic quantity rather than as a strong leg plus a weak tilt. Using ABS(oancf) in the denominator removes the sign-flip defect: a cash-burning firm scores near -1 and additional external issuance pushes it further toward -1 rather than making it look better, so the signal bites hardest exactly where the hypothesis predicts.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ma( ratio( oancf, add( abs( oancf ), add( sstk, dltis ) ) ), 3 )

input_signals.name: Uncovered Payout Financed By New Capital
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvt), ib), at)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltis, sstk), dltr), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Distributions that exceed reported earnings are sustainable only if not simultaneously backfilled with fresh external capital; firms that pay out more than they earn while raising net new debt and equity are recycling investors' own money and should underperform, whereas uncovered payout accompanied by debt retirement reflects genuine balance-sheet slack.
input_signals.reasoning: The coverage shortfall is now measured against earnings (payout − ib), not against operating cash flow, so the expression no longer contains the ib − oancf accrual construct the critic flagged as a rediscovery. The financing leg is industry-standardized and mean-zero, so the payout-shortfall rank serves only as a magnitude gate and the signal's sign is determined by whether the firm is a net raiser or net retirer of capital — the composite is therefore not monotone in either single-theme leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( add( prstkc, dvt ), ib ), at ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( dltis, sstk ), dltr ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capital Absorbed Without Profit Improvement
input_signals.expression: SUB(RANK(TREND(RATIO(oiadp, at), 5)), RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(ADD(sstk, dltis), 5), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that have cumulatively absorbed large amounts of outside equity and debt over five years without a corresponding upward trend in operating profitability have destroyed capital and are overvalued; firms improving profitability while raising nothing are self-funding real gains.
input_signals.reasoning: The accepted gen-0 trend signal paired a five-year profit trend with a one-year debt change, mismatching horizons and yielding a weak alpha; matching the financing measure to the same five-year window with cumulative gross issuance converts it into a capital-productivity test. Cumulative multi-year issuance is also far more persistent than annual issuance, which should reduce portfolio turnover and raise the reliability of the long-short alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( rank( trend( ratio( oiadp, at ), 5 ) ), rank( ratio( ts_sum( add( sstk, dltis ), 5 ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Verified Cash Generation With Verified Distribution
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvt), sstk), 3), at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(oancf, 3), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Underpriced cash generation requires both facts to be true at once over a multi-year window: the firm must actually have produced cash from operations, and it must actually have handed cash back net of new equity; either alone is uninformative, since debt-financed distributions and hoarded cash flow are both common.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the ratio-with-ABS-denominator by a MIN of two industry-standardized three-year flows removes the pathology the critic identified — a cash-burning firm now scores at its (very negative) cash-flow z-score no matter how much debt-financed cash it distributes, so it cannot enter the long leg. It also stops being a payout-ratio variant: the score is the weaker of two independently measured cumulative flows, which is a conjunction rather than a quotient, and both legs remain continuous with no point mass.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( ts_sum( sub( add( prstkc, dvt ), sstk ), 3 ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( ts_sum( oancf, 3 ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cash Flow Coverage Of Short Term Debt
input_signals.expression: RATIO(SUB(MA(oancf, 3), dlc), ADD(ABS(MA(oancf, 3)), ADD(dlc, 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Debt in current liabilities is the balance of financing that must actually be refinanced or repaid within the year; firms whose normalized operating cash flow exceeds that obligation are insulated from credit-market conditions and can distribute freely, whereas firms whose near-term obligations dwarf internal cash are rollover-dependent and exposed to funding shocks the market underweights in calm periods.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that dltr is realized debt reduction rather than scheduled maturities; dlc is the actual stock of short-maturity obligations, so the revised expression measures rollover exposure rather than penalizing deleveraging. Smoothing operating cash flow over three years makes the coverage measure reflect normalized earning power rather than a single year's working-capital swing, and the bounded [-1, 1] form keeps cash-burning firms pinned near the floor.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( ma( oancf, 3 ), dlc ), add( abs( ma( oancf, 3 ) ), add( dlc, 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Debt Service Capacity After Interest Burden
input_signals.expression: RATIO(SUB(MA(oibdp, 3), xint), ADD(ABS(MA(oibdp, 3)), ADD(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Operating profit left over after paying the cost of existing debt, measured against the stock of debt itself, is the market's slowest-updating measure of solvency; firms generating ample post-interest profit per dollar of debt have capital-structure slack that supports future distributions, while firms whose profits are consumed by interest are effectively working for creditors.
input_signals.reasoning: This shifts the coverage mechanism from a cash-timing question (can I repay maturing principal?) to a price-of-capital question (does the business out-earn its financing cost?), using the interest expense channel that no archive signal has touched. Because oibdp, xint, dltt and dlc are income-statement and balance-sheet items rather than cash-flow-statement flows, coverage should exceed the roughly 0.09 typical of the prstkc/sstk constructs.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( ma( oibdp, 3 ), xint ), add( abs( ma( oibdp, 3 ) ), add( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cash Generative With Long Dated Debt
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(dlc, ADD(ADD(dlc, dltt), 1))), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Financial autonomy requires both a cash engine and a debt structure that does not force the firm back to the market soon; the maturity *composition* of debt, independent of how much debt there is, determines how often management must submit to credit-market conditions.
input_signals.reasoning: This separates the scale of obligations (already captured by the gen-2 coverage ratio) from their maturity mix, testing whether short-dated funding structure is a distinct risk channel rather than a proxy for having too much debt relative to cash. The MIN enforces the conjunction the hypothesis states — a firm cannot enter the long leg on cash flow alone or on long maturities alone — and both legs are continuous industry z-scores, avoiding the point masses that destabilized the indicator constructs.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_zscore( winsor( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( neg( ratio( dlc, add( add( dlc, dltt ), 1 ) ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Stress Year Coverage Of Near Term Debt
input_signals.expression: RATIO(SUB(TS_MIN(oancf, 3), dlc), ADD(ABS(TS_MIN(oancf, 3)), ADD(dlc, 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Refinancing risk is realized in bad years, so what matters is whether the firm's *worst* recent year of operating cash flow would still have covered its near-maturity debt; firms that pass this stress test never have to approach credit markets from weakness, while firms that pass only on average are one bad year away from dilutive or distressed financing.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than adding a small, collinear dividend term to the archive's best coverage ratio, this replaces the central-tendency measure of cash flow with a tail statistic, which is a different economic claim: two firms with identical three-year average coverage are now separated by the volatility of their cash generation relative to their funding calendar. The change is attributable — any improvement over the parent is due to downside cash-flow risk interacting with near-term obligations, not to a rescaling of the same two quantities.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( ts_min( oancf, 3 ), dlc ), add( abs( ts_min( oancf, 3 ) ), add( dlc, 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Funding Autonomy With Revealed Distribution
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(MA(oancf, 3), dlc), ADD(ABS(MA(oancf, 3)), ADD(dlc, 1))), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvt), ADD(sstk, dltis)), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital returned to shareholders is credible evidence of underpriced cash generation only when the firm is not simultaneously obliged to the credit market; a distribution from a firm whose maturing debt exceeds its operating cash flow is a transfer from creditors, whereas a distribution from a firm with funding autonomy is genuine surplus.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive shows a sharp split — coverage-type signals produce reliable FF5 alpha (5.2% at t=3.68) while net-payout constructs produce strong Fama-MacBeth slopes but almost no alpha — and the natural diagnosis is that unconditional payout is spanned by RMW/CMA while payout backed by funding autonomy is not. MIN enforces the conjunction so a firm cannot enter the long leg on coverage alone or payout alone, which directly tests whether the payout theme adds anything once the funding-obligation state is controlled.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( ma( oancf, 3 ), dlc ), add( abs( ma( oancf, 3 ) ), add( dlc, 1 ) ) ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( prstkc, dvt ), add( sstk, dltis ) ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Persistent Coverage Of Near Term Obligations
input_signals.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(oancf, dlc), 0), 5), RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(oancf, 3), dlc), ADD(ABS(MA(oancf, 3)), ADD(dlc, 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that has covered its near-term debt out of operating cash in every one of the last five years has demonstrated structural funding independence, whereas a firm that covers today but failed twice recently is a cyclical borrower whose current coverage will not survive the next downturn; the market prices the current state and underweights the track record.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's coverage family has been tested only as a current level, a tail, and a change, never as a frequency, and the frequency statistic captures a different economic property — reliability of the funding position across states of the world. Multiplying the 0-5 count by the continuous current-coverage rank supplies a within-bucket tiebreaker, avoiding the lumpy decile boundaries that plausibly produced the perverse Sharpe of the gen-0 count construct and the null gen-1 signed count.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ts_sum( indicator( sub( oancf, dlc ), 0 ), 5 ), rank( ratio( sub( ma( oancf, 3 ), dlc ), add( abs( ma( oancf, 3 ) ), add( dlc, 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Internally Funded Debt Retirement
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The clearest evidence of underpriced cash generation on the debt side is a firm that both produces strong operating cash and uses it to retire more debt than it raises; such firms shrink creditor claims on future cash flow without any market transaction, whereas cash-generative firms that keep rolling debt forward are recycling rather than earning.
input_signals.reasoning: The theme's "return capital" idea has been tested almost entirely through the equity channel (buybacks, dividends, share issuance); this is its debt-channel counterpart, and paired with Signal 1 it tells us whether conditioned capital return works through repaying creditors, through paying shareholders, or both. Using dltr as a *use of internal cash* rather than as a proxy for scheduled maturities repairs the gen-2 misuse of that variable that the critic correctly identified.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_zscore( winsor( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( dltr, dltis ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Creditor Claims Outgrowing Cash Generation
input_signals.expression: RATIO(SUB(DELTA(MA(oancf, 3), 1), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), ADD(ABS(DELTA(MA(oancf, 3), 1)), ADD(ABS(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Solvency is a race between two flows: the cash the business generates and the creditor claims stacked against it; a firm whose normalized operating cash flow is growing faster than its debt stock is widening its funding cushion regardless of where the level sits, while a firm adding debt faster than cash flow is consuming cushion and will eventually have to finance on the market's terms.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than swapping the denominator of the archive's level-coverage ratio, this changes the object being measured from a stock position to the relative growth rates of the two competing flows, so it is informative even for firms whose current coverage is unremarkable and it is not spanned by the gen-3 debt-service-capacity level. The symmetric bounded form keeps the measure scale-free and comparable across firm sizes, and it treats a firm that shrinks debt while cash flow falls differently from one that grows both.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( delta( ma( oancf, 3 ), 1 ), delta( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ) ), add( abs( delta( ma( oancf, 3 ), 1 ) ), add( abs( delta( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Self Funded Innovation With Capital Return
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvt), ADD(sstk, dltis)), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that sustains heavy research spending and still returns capital net of all issuance is generating far more cash than its reported earnings suggest, because R&D is expensed; the market anchors on the depressed earnings and misses that the firm is simultaneously funding its future and paying owners.
input_signals.reasoning: Every archive construct has used realized profits or cash flow as the operating leg; using expensed intangible investment as the operating-strength proxy is a distinct channel, and its interaction with net payout identifies firms whose apparent low profitability is an accounting artifact rather than an economic fact. Treating unreported R&D as zero is the standard and economically correct convention, so coverage is set by the payout leg rather than by R&D reporting.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( prstkc, dvt ), add( sstk, dltis ) ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Stress Test Of Interest And Maturities
input_signals.expression: RATIO(SUB(SUB(TS_MIN(oancf, 3), xint), dlc), ADD(ABS(TS_MIN(oancf, 3)), ADD(ADD(dlc, xint), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The full creditor claim on a firm's cash in any given year is interest plus maturing principal, and the binding question is whether the firm can meet that claim in a bad year of its own cash generation; firms clearing this combined stress test never negotiate from weakness, while firms failing it face either dilution or forced deleveraging.
input_signals.reasoning: Two ingredients have independently produced reliable alpha — the worst-year cash-flow numerator (4.6%, t=3.09) and the interest-burden channel (3.2%, t=3.00) — and this states the complete debt-service identity rather than pairing them mechanically: interest and current maturities are the same year's cash obligation and belong in one claim total. It also fixes the denominator criticism of the gen-3 interest signal, since numerator and denominator now describe the same object, cash available versus cash owed.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( sub( ts_min( oancf, 3 ), xint ), dlc ), add( abs( ts_min( oancf, 3 ) ), add( add( dlc, xint ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Recurring Fixed Charge Coverage
input_signals.expression: RATIO(SUB(MA(oancf, 3), ADD(xint, dvt)), ADD(ABS(MA(oancf, 3)), ADD(ADD(xint, dvt), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Maturing principal is lumpy and often refinanced automatically, but interest and dividends are recurring commitments that must be paid every year from operations; firms whose normalized cash flow comfortably exceeds this recurring charge have real discretionary capacity, while firms that barely cover it are one bad year from a dividend cut or a covenant problem.
input_signals.reasoning: This is not an input substitution in the archive's coverage ratio: the obligation set changes from a repayable stock to the annual fixed charges that creditors and shareholders both expect, which is a different economic claim about which commitments discipline the firm. It also gives the payout theme a role the archive has not tested — dividends as a *burden* to be covered rather than as a signal of surplus — and pairs it with the interest channel that has already shown independent alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( ma( oancf, 3 ), add( xint, dvt ) ), add( abs( ma( oancf, 3 ) ), add( add( xint, dvt ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Distributions Funded By Borrowing Not Earnings
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dvt, prstkc), at), 1)), MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(GROWTH(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The clearest case of financing behavior masking weakness is a firm distributing heavily to shareholders while expanding its debt and generating little operating cash; the payout maintains the appearance of health, the borrowing pays for it, and the deterioration surfaces only when credit tightens.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than a profitability-gated change in short-term debt — which the gen-3 maturity signal already showed to be uninformative — this requires all three conditions simultaneously, so the extreme leg is a specific and economically coherent population rather than a generic debt-growth or issuance sort. The three-way MIN also guarantees non-monotonicity in each individual theme: high payout alone, high debt growth alone, or weak cash flow alone leaves a firm in the middle of the distribution.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( add( dvt, prstkc ), at ), 1 ) ), min( ind_zscore( winsor( growth( add( dltt, dlc ), 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( neg( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Funds From Operations Fixed Charge Coverage
input_signals.expression: RATIO(SUB(MA(ADD(ib, dp), 3), ADD(xint, dvt)), ADD(ABS(MA(ADD(ib, dp), 3)), ADD(ADD(xint, dvt), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The economic content of fixed-charge coverage is whether the business throws off enough recurring internal funds to service its recurring claims, and funds from operations — income plus depreciation — measures that as well as the cash-flow statement does while being observable for far more firms and far earlier years.
input_signals.reasoning: Every strong signal in this archive is capped near 0.08-0.09 coverage because oancf requires a modern cash-flow statement, and that thin sample is the most likely reason strong cross-sectional slopes translate into only moderate portfolio precision. Substituting ib+dp is not a cosmetic input swap but a deliberate sample-extension test: if the mechanism is real it should survive on a proxy that predates SFAS 95, and the wider cross-section should tighten the long-short alpha's standard error.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( ma( add( ib, dp ), 3 ), add( xint, dvt ) ), add( abs( ma( add( ib, dp ), 3 ) ), add( add( xint, dvt ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Debt Amortization Capacity From Free Cash
input_signals.expression: RATIO(SUB(MA(oancf, 3), ADD(xint, dvt)), ADD(ADD(dltt, dlc), ABS(SUB(MA(oancf, 3), ADD(xint, dvt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The cash a firm keeps after interest and dividends is the only cash available to retire debt, so expressing that residual as a fraction of the debt stock measures how quickly the firm could extinguish creditor claims entirely; firms that could self-liquidate their debt in a few years hold real strategic optionality, while firms whose residual is trivial against their debt are permanently financed by lenders.
input_signals.reasoning: This avoids the additive-union problem the critic identified: dlc no longer sits in the numerator alongside much smaller recurring charges but appears in the denominator as part of the stock being amortized, so the measure asks a different question (speed of debt extinguishment) rather than re-stating annual coverage. The bounded [-1, 1] form handles firms with negative residual cash correctly, and it links the recurring-charge mechanism that produced the archive's best alpha to the debt-stock dimension that the coverage family has only measured as a maturity calendar.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( ma( oancf, 3 ), add( xint, dvt ) ), add( add( dltt, dlc ), abs( sub( ma( oancf, 3 ), add( xint, dvt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Repurchases Backed By Discretionary Surplus
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(MA(oancf, 3), ADD(xint, dvt)), at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(prstkc, at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A repurchase is credible evidence of underpriced cash generation only when the firm also has substantial cash left after servicing creditors and maintaining its dividend; buybacks by firms with no discretionary surplus are financed by borrowing or by starving other claims and carry no positive information.
input_signals.reasoning: This removes the ABS pathology the critic identified — the surplus now enters monotonically as its own standardized leg, so larger surplus always raises the score and the top decile is firms with both a big post-commitment cushion and large repurchases. The conjunction is also the sharpest available test of the theme's central claim, since the long leg is exactly "profitable firm returning capital it can demonstrably spare" and the short leg is firms failing on whichever dimension is weaker.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( ma( oancf, 3 ), add( xint, dvt ) ), at ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( prstkc, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Post Commitment Free Cash Margin
input_signals.expression: RATIO(SUB(MA(oancf, 3), ADD(xint, dvt)), ADD(MA(sale, 3), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: The cash a business retains after paying creditors and shareholders, expressed per dollar of revenue, is the purest measure of how much surplus the operating model actually throws off; two firms with the same coverage ratio differ economically if one earns that surplus on a thin revenue base and the other on a large one.
input_signals.reasoning: The champion ratio is self-normalizing, which compresses the extremes — every firm with large cash flow relative to charges maps toward +1 regardless of how large the surplus is relative to the business — whereas a revenue deflator preserves magnitude and gives a smoothly distributed margin variable that sorts more finely into deciles. This isolates the deflator design choice with a clear economic reading (free cash margin after capital-provider claims) rather than substituting an input.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( ma( oancf, 3 ), add( xint, dvt ) ), add( ma( sale, 3 ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Uncovered Commitments Met By New Capital
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(MA(oancf, 3), ADD(xint, dvt)), ADD(ABS(MA(oancf, 3)), ADD(ADD(xint, dvt), 1)))), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The failure mode the theme predicts is a firm whose operations do not cover its recurring obligations and which therefore turns to the capital markets to bridge the gap; such firms are financing yesterday's promises with tomorrow's dilution, and their apparent access to funding masks a deteriorating franchise.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's short legs have generally been weaker than its long legs because they were built by negating a long-leg construct, whereas this requires a specific joint condition — commitment shortfall *and* active external raising — that identifies forced financing rather than opportunistic issuance. Both legs are continuous industry z-scores, so the extreme decile is stable and neither leg alone can drive the sort.
input_signals.author: proposer
